set.beta: Jötnar follows a continuous crack system on the left side of the North Norwegian Buttress, roughly 100 yards left of the original 1980s aid line. It is a 16-pitch big wall at VI 5.9 A3+, mostly aid: thin pins, beaks, hooks and rivets, with free sections up to 5.9+. The two aid cruxes are P4 (A3+) and P9 (A3). Natural ledges are few, so a portaledge is required. The tops of P3 and P6 make good ledge camps. Every belay is bolted stainless steel except P15, which is a gear belay. Climb it late July to early September. Before that, snowmelt turns P5 and P6 into a waterfall in the afternoon, so climb them in the morning. Rack: double set of nuts and cams from micronuts to a #4 Camalot plus one #5, a set of offsets, 5 beaks, 2 Lost Arrows, 10 rivet hangers (some rivets are deep and need the #1 size), 2 sets of hooks, and a ledge fly and rain shell for the middle of the wall.
set.overview: The North Norwegian Buttress is a roughly 2,000-foot buttress on Mount Index's northeast face, plainly visible from US 2 above Lake Serene. A deep cleft between the Main and Middle summits separates it from the smaller South Norwegian Buttress. For decades it saw almost no traffic: a 1980s solo aid line and the 2002 Voodoo Project were its only routes, and neither has been repeated. Jötnar (VI 5.9 A3+, 16 pitches) was climbed in 2020 capsule-style over two trips and 14 days. This page describes Jötnar. The bolted free line Bluebell (5.13-), freed in 2023, is a separate route on the same buttress.
set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling Jötnar from its bolted stations. There is no walk-off. Many pitches overhang, so expect to swing in or clip directional gear to reach the next anchor. P7 overhangs more than 40 ft: leave a fixed line on it during the ascent, or be ready to down-aid it on the way down. P15's climbing belay is on gear, and its bolted rappel anchor sits at the far right end of the same ledge. Strip every fixed line as you go rather than leaving it on the wall. From the base, reverse the talus traverse around Lake Serene to the maintained trail.
set.rappels: Rappel the route from its bolted stainless anchors. P15 is the one gear belay, and its bolted rappel anchor is at the far right of that ledge. Overhanging pitches need swings or directionals, and P7 needs a fixed line or down-aiding.
set.fa: Sam Boyce, Lani Chapko and Kyle Willis, August 2020 (capsule style, two trips, 14 days on the wall)

pitch_detail.notes: Wandering, poorly protected face climbing (5.7 R) up to the huge right-trending ramp system visible from Lake Serene. Where it starts depends on the snowpack. On the first ascent it began a couple of hundred metres right of the main watercourse, out of a shallow moat. Belay at a bolted anchor.

Easy free climbing up a small ramp, then steep cracks and thin aid on the face below a splitter, finishing on a large ledge. Much of the original A4 R section has deteriorated. This pitch can be linked with P3.
Clean splitter cracks to a sheltered, slabby belay. The belay is a good portaledge site, sheltered from above.

The aid crux. Climb an A3 left-facing crack with a roof halfway up. Hook out under the loose-looking roof block to reach a crack that takes beaks well, then exit right on hooks to a stance below the muddy corner.
A left-facing corner below a slab. Snowmelt turns it into a waterfall from the afternoon on, so aim to be on it early in the morning. Linking it with P6 is recommended.
Easy slab, then a thin seam and A2 face climbing with a lot of hooking to the belay, which makes an excellent portaledge bivy.
Rivets up a left-facing corner lead into wildly steep cracks. The pitch overhangs more than 40 ft, so fix a line here for the descent, or plan to down-aid it. A 40 m rope reaches the next belay.

The Fang Roof. Start on A2, then take a beautiful splitter hand crack out through the overhang. It is aided at C1 here, though it would go free at about 5.10. Exit with 5.9 free climbing to the belay.

The second aid crux. Go right of the vegetation and aid up on thin pins, rivets and many hooks. A long bat-hook section avoids a chossy corner. Near the top, at a bolt, either tension traverse right or make a big reach to beak placements.
Follow a shallow right-facing flake trending left beneath a huge hanging roof and arête. Tension traverse left using hooks and short free sections to the belay.
Pass a bolt into a crack and follow it to its end, then easy free climbing to a good grassy ledge.

The Headwall. Free climb (5.8) straight up to a bolt, traverse right into a chimney hole, and hook out of a roof on hooks and rivets. Tricky beaks lead to a long rivet ladder with occasional free moves. Avoid hauling above this pitch if you can.
Free climbing off the belay on thin gear, then trend left along a crack past a short rivet ladder and a false belay. Weave back right to a good ledge on the crest of the buttress.
Runout face climbing straight off the belay through broken ledges near the buttress crest. Two trees guard the belay, and the climbing stays close to the crest.

Traverse a long way left to a large right-facing corner. Free it at about 5.10 or aid it at C1 on roots, then grovel through cedars to a large ledge. The only gear belay on the route takes finger to hand sizes. The bolted rappel anchor is at the far right end of this ledge.
A mossy 5.7 dihedral and a gully lead to the top of the buttress.

review.climb: Jötnar (VI 5.9 A3+, 16 pitches, 2,000 ft; FA Boyce, Chapko and Willis, August 2020). The name 'North Norwegian Buttress' is the wall, not a route, so it is ambiguous. Two lines on the buttress are documented pitch by pitch: Jötnar and Bluebell. Jötnar matches every classification column the row holds: grade 5.9, pitches 16, length_m 610 (Jötnar is given as 606 m), discipline alpine. Bluebell would need the grade, the pitch count and the table changed, and its pitch count is itself disputed (17 against 21). The row's stored table, rappels and part of its descent described Bluebell, and its fa named the 1980s aid line.
review.changed: beta, overview, descent_text, rappels and fa now describe Jötnar. The old table (6 Bluebell sections, with sentence grades) is replaced by Jötnar's 16 pitches, with grades, lengths (ft converted to m) and anchors as given on the route's topo page. crux is set on P4 only, the pitch the topo names as the aid crux. P9 is called the 'second crux' in its notes but not flagged. P16 has no anchor field because none is stated. approach is kept: it describes the shared Lake Serene approach to the buttress cirque and nothing specific to Bluebell. Nothing was added that is not in the sources. Dropped: the overview's Bluebell pitch counts and the descent's unsourced '9-10 single-strand rappels' and 'nearly as long as the climb'.

name.evidence: The buttress name identifies no single line. Jötnar is the line whose grade, pitch count and length the row already stores (MP: VI 5.9 A3+, 2,000 ft/606 m, 16 pitches; AAJ 2021 agrees on 2,000 ft, 16 pitches, VI 5.9 A3+).

grade.evidence: The stored '5.9' leaves out the aid rating. The route is mostly aid, with an A3+ crux on P4 (MP topo; AAJ gives VI 5.9 A3+).

review.other_findings: pro_needs could not be read (show.mjs does not print it). If it holds Bluebell's rack ('16 draws', '70 m rope'), replace it with Jötnar's rack, now stated in beta: double nuts and cams micronut to #4 plus a single #5, offsets, 5 beaks, 2 Lost Arrows, 10 rivet hangers, 2 sets of hooks, portaledge. Bluebell itself has a full pitch-by-pitch description on MP (17 pitches, 5.13-, fully bolted). If the owner wants it in the catalog, it should be a NEW row on this area, not this one.

wa_mount_index_north_peak_traverse.skip_reason: DUPLICATE of wa_traverse_of_mount_index. Every column except beta describes the North Face of North Index followed by the full North–Middle–Main traverse, and the row sits on the same area with the same grade (5.7+) and length (1524 m). The name 'Main Peak via North Approach' matches no separately documented climb.

review.climb: The row's id (north_peak_traverse), overview, approach, pitch_detail (North Face ascent → North to Middle → Middle Peak → Middle to Main), rappels and fa (Beckey and Schoening, 1950) all describe the Index Traverse, the climb wa_traverse_of_mount_index already holds with a far better 9-section breakdown. Only the name and the one-sentence beta point elsewhere. The documented ways onto Main Peak are the standard east/southeast side from Lake Serene (Hourglass Gully / East Ridge, already in the catalog as wa_hourglass_gully_winter for its winter form) and a long brushy western approach from Proctor Creek over 'Persindex' (Pk 5360+). Neither is a 'north approach', and the beta gives nothing about either beyond naming them. The only line that reaches Main Peak from the north is the traverse itself. So the row adds nothing the traverse row lacks. The beta's claim of 'mixed Class 4-5 scrambling' on the East Route has no source.
review.changed: Nothing written. Recommend deleting the row.
review.other_findings: Before deleting: this row's descent_text sends the party down from Main Peak by the East Ridge / Hourglass Gully. The surviving row's descent_text ('Rappel from three peaks back down the route… 2-3 hour descent from Main Peak') was already marked UNCLEAR in verify-5. None of the sources read here (the MP traverse page, one traverse report) says how parties get off Main Peak after the traverse, so neither text could be confirmed, and neither is moved. This row's descent_text also contains a quoted party ('no rap stations on this side of the bowl'), which is testimony. It should not be carried over as written. If the owner wants a standalone Main Peak summer route (Hourglass Gully / East Ridge), that is a new row, and it needs its own research.

pitch_detail.notes: The face is the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's eastern cirque, between Liberty Ridge and Curtis Ridge. The lower lines start from the upper Carbon Glacier, reached up the glacier from the Carbon River side or across it from a camp near the foot of Liberty Ridge (about 8,600 ft). Some upper-wall link-ups instead come in from the White River side, over St. Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier to a high camp on Curtis Ridge, then traverse onto the face.

A very large bergschrund guards the foot of the wall. Above it, three ribs (West, Central and East) give the only relief from the avalanche and rockfall paths between them. Expect steep snow faces around 45° broken by rock bands and small buttresses. The Central Rib carries the most rockfall, and all but the westernmost line sit under active seracs.

Higher up, the ribs give way to mixed rock and ice, then ice steps of 50–60°, beneath a 200–300 ft ice cliff that caps the whole face and sheds ice onto the lines below. A crevasse can run the width of the ice cap here. Lines either climb through the cliff to the summit plateau near Liberty Cap, or traverse beneath it (the Traverse of the Angels) to exit onto Liberty Ridge or Curtis Ridge.

review.climb: The Willis Wall as a face, described at overview level. The row's name is the face, and no single line on it (West Rib 1961, East Rib 1963, Central Rib 1965, the 1970 winter Brumal Buttress line, and the Curtis Ridge upper-wall link-ups) has a pitch- or section-level description anywhere. Picking one would mean inventing its breakdown. The lines share a documented structure: glacier approach, bergschrund, rib below the ice cliff, then the ice cliff or a traverse under it. The row can describe the face honestly if its table stays at that level. overview, beta, approach, descent_text and fa already describe the face as a whole and are left as they are. fa names the first ascent of the wall (West Rib, 1961), which is correct at face level.
review.changed: The 3-entry table is kept at 3 entries, and the 'Approach traverse' label is kept. Its note was specific to the Winthrop/Curtis Ridge link-up; it now gives both documented approaches. 'Lower wall' is now 'Bergschrund and lower ribs': the unsourced 'M5+' chip is removed, and the note names the three ribs and their hazards. 'Upper wall / ice cliff' is now 'Upper wall and ice cliff': its sentence-length chip is replaced by a terrain chip, and the note names the ice cliff height and the two ways lines finish. No lengths, crux flags or grades beyond what the sources state.

name.evidence: Keep. The row describes the face, and every column now does.

review.other_findings: MP grades its single 'Willis Wall' entry M5+ X, but that entry covers a specific link-up (FA credited to Bell with a Traverse of the Angels link-up, and to Klubberud/Campbell), not the lower wall. So the old table's 'M5+' on the lower wall is not supported, and it has been removed. rappels ends with 'see the ropework note', which points at nothing on the page; worth a separate prose pass. The approach column's Fairfax Bridge closure date (April 2025) was not checked here.

wa_lemah_two_scramble.skip_reason: DUPLICATE of wa_lemah_mountain_east_route. Every stage of the row (Pete Lake, PCT, Lemah Creek meadow, glacier remnant, cliff bands, chute, the col between Lemah Two and Lemah Main) is the standard route to Lemah MAIN. No source describes going from that col up to Lemah Two's own summit. The row's Lemah Two finish is undocumented.

review.climb: The standard southeast route to Lemah Mountain's main summit (Lemah 3). Every description found takes it up the glacier remnant and Class 2-3 cliff bands, or up the snow slope and crux chute around Lemah Two's east buttress, to the col between Lemah Two and Lemah Main. From there it turns NORTH to the main summit block. Lemah Two is only passed below. The row's only material of its own is its last step, 'from the col, turn south / a short 3rd-4th class rock section to Lemah Two's summit', in beta, pitch_detail ('Col to summit') and descent_text. No source supports it: the only mention of Lemah Two's own summit is a general statement that each of the five summits has its own route, with no description. The likely origin is that older USGS maps mark Lemah Two as the high point of Lemah Mountain, so the main route got filed on it. Stripping the invented finish would leave a route that ends at a col, which is wa_lemah_mountain_east_route minus its summit.
review.changed: Nothing written. Recommend deleting the row. LEAVE would keep a Class 3-4 summit finish that no source describes.
review.other_findings: The sibling row wa_lemah_two_goatshead_spire has an overview describing the spire as 'distinct from the standard walk-up/scramble to Lemah Two's main summit'. That scramble is undocumented too, so the phrase should go in the same pass as this deletion. The area wa_lemah_two would then hold only Goatshead Spire.

wa_mount_carrie_standard.skip_reason: DUPLICATE of wa_mount_carrie_se_route. Read as the standard route, which its approach and pitch_detail describe, this row is the High Divide → Catwalk → Boston Charlie's → southwest ridge scramble that wa_mount_carrie_se_route already holds in full. Read as a Carrie Glacier ascent, it has no source at all: no documented route climbs the Carrie Glacier to the summit.

review.climb: The standard route up Mount Carrie. Sources describe it as a non-glacial scramble: Sol Duc trailhead, Heart Lake, the High Divide, Cat Peak and the Class 3 Catwalk, Boston Charlie's Camp, then the grassy southwest ridge (class 1) to a scree basin and a class 2 scree/snow traverse to the true summit at the far right of the basin. It needs an ice axe, not a rope. The name's 'Carrie Glacier' part and the beta's roped glacier travel in the northeast cirque do not describe any documented ascent. The glacier sits in the NE cirque and flows north-northeast away from the Catwalk approach, between an arête and Mount Fairchild. Bailey Range parties who carry glacier gear use it for the Fairchild Glacier beyond the summit, not to climb Carrie. The beta reads like a description of the glacier itself (its elevations, flow and confining arête), turned into a route. With the glacier material removed, this row is the same climb as wa_mount_carrie_se_route, whose pitch_detail, beta, approach, descent_text and rappels already describe that line.
review.changed: Nothing written. Recommend deleting this row and keeping wa_mount_carrie_se_route.
review.other_findings: The surviving row has the wrong NAME: wa_mount_carrie_se_route is called 'Southeast Route via Hurricane Ridge / Cat Basin', and its own overview says no route connects Hurricane Ridge to Carrie. A rename to something like 'Southwest Ridge via High Divide and the Catwalk' should go with this deletion; its id would stay. This row's fa ('Probably Billy Everett, 1885') was not verified and is not on the surviving row. If the owner wants it kept, verify it first. This row's approach column is slightly more detailed than the survivor's, but the facts are the same, so nothing needs merging.
